question: Which control plane component is the single entry point that validates all requests and persists state to etcd?
choices: kube-scheduler
kube-apiserver
kube-controller-manager
kubelet
explanation: The kube-apiserver is the only front door — every kubectl command, internal call, and webhook flows through it, and it persists state to etcd. The scheduler only places pods, the controller-manager runs reconciliation loops, and the kubelet is a node agent; none of these are the cluster's entry point or talk to etcd directly.

question: In which directory does the kubelet watch for the static pod manifests of the control plane components?
choices: /etc/kubernetes/manifests
/etc/kubernetes/pki
/var/lib/kubelet/manifests
/etc/containerd
explanation: The kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests and starts any static pods defined there (kube-apiserver.yaml, etcd.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml). /etc/kubernetes/pki holds certificates, /etc/containerd holds the runtime config, and /var/lib/kubelet/manifests is not the kubeadm default path.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — What kubeadm init creates

question: A pod fails to receive an IP address and the node reports NetworkPluginNotReady. Which extension interface is responsible?
choices: CRI
CSI
CRD
CNI
explanation: The CNI (Container Network Interface) gives pods their IPs and configures pod-to-pod routing; a missing or broken CNI causes NetworkPluginNotReady and NotReady nodes. CRI is the runtime interface (container won't start), CSI is storage (PV pending), and CRD is an API extension mechanism, not a networking interface.

question: You are preparing an Ubuntu host for kubeadm. Why must net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables be set to 1?
choices: To enable swap accounting for the scheduler
To make bridged Layer-2 traffic visible to iptables so kube-proxy and CNI rules work
To allow containerd to use OverlayFS image layers
To open port 6443 for the API server
explanation: This sysctl makes bridged L2 traffic visible to iptables/netfilter, which kube-proxy and CNI plug-ins rely on; it's a hard kubeadm requirement and defaults to 0 on stock Ubuntu. Swap is handled by swapoff, OverlayFS is enabled by the overlay kernel module, and port 6443 is unrelated to this sysctl.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Kernel modules and sysctl

question: After a clean kubeadm init, containerd and the kubelet appear to start but pods crash-loop and logs are misleading. What is the most likely root cause?
choices: The pod-network-CIDR is too small
Swap was left enabled
The cgroup driver mismatch — SystemdCgroup is not set to true in containerd
The API server certificate expired
explanation: containerd ships with SystemdCgroup = false but the kubelet uses the systemd cgroup driver; a mismatch makes pods crash-loop while logs point at the wrong layer. A small CIDR or enabled swap produce different, more obvious failures, and a fresh cluster's certs are valid.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — containerd and the CRI

question: Which kubeadm init flag is the most common silent cause of broken cross-node pod communication?
choices: --upload-certs
--apiserver-advertise-address
--pod-network-cidr not matching the CNI's expected range
--kubernetes-version
explanation: If --pod-network-cidr doesn't match what the CNI expects (e.g., Calico's 192.168.0.0/16), pods get IPs but can't route across nodes — a silent timeout with no clean error. --upload-certs handles cert distribution, --apiserver-advertise-address sets the bind interface, and --kubernetes-version pins the version; none cause this silent routing failure.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — kubeadm init flags that matter

question: Immediately after kubeadm init (before installing a CNI), what is the expected state of the nodes and CoreDNS?
choices: All nodes Ready, CoreDNS Running
Nodes NotReady and CoreDNS Pending — this is correct, not a failure
Nodes Ready but CoreDNS CrashLoopBackOff
The API server is down until the CNI is installed
explanation: The kubelet won't mark a node Ready until a CNI can assign pod IPs, and CoreDNS needs a pod IP to start, so NotReady nodes and Pending CoreDNS are expected. The control plane static pods use host networking and run fine; installing the CNI flips nodes to Ready in ~30 seconds. Misreading this as a failure wastes exam time.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — From init to ready

question: How does kubeadm join provide two-way verification when a worker joins the cluster?
choices: The worker and API server exchange SSH keys
Username and password over HTTPS
The kubelet certificate is manually copied to every node
A bootstrap token authenticates the worker, and the CA cert hash lets the worker verify the API server
explanation: The short-lived bootstrap token proves the worker is allowed to join, while --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash (SHA-256 of the CA cert) lets the worker confirm it's talking to the genuine control plane, preventing a man-in-the-middle. There are no SSH keys or passwords in this flow, and the kubelet cert is auto-generated via CSR, not hand-copied.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Bootstrap tokens and join workflow

question: You lost the join command printed by kubeadm init. Which command regenerates a complete, ready-to-paste join command?
choices: kubeadm token create --print-join-command
kubeadm init phase bootstrap-token
kubeadm certs renew all
kubectl get bootstraptokens
explanation: kubeadm token create --print-join-command emits a full join command with a fresh token and the correct CA cert hash. The other options don't produce a ready-to-use join command: 'certs renew' rotates certificates, and there's no kubectl resource that prints the assembled join string.
source: Installing Clusters with kubeadm — Managing kubeconfig

question: A Kubernetes context bundles which three elements?
choices: Node, pod, namespace
API version, kind, metadata
Cluster, user, and default namespace
CA cert, token, kubeconfig path
explanation: A context is a named tuple of a cluster (API endpoint + CA), a user (identity/credentials), and a default namespace. The other options describe pod manifest fields or arbitrary pieces; they are not the definition of a context.

question: Why is 'kubectl config use-context' a safe first command for every exam task even if the cluster is unreachable?
choices: It only reads and writes your local kubeconfig file, not the cluster
It restarts the API server
It validates RBAC permissions remotely
It refreshes the bootstrap token
explanation: kubectl config commands operate purely on the local ~/.kube/config file and don't contact the API server, so they succeed regardless of cluster state — making them the ideal first step after each question to avoid running work against the wrong cluster.
source: Kubernetes Foundations — When to use YAML instead of imperative

question: A task requires granting a user read access to pods only within the 'frontend' namespace. Which combination should you use?
choices: ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding
Role + RoleBinding in the frontend namespace
ClusterRole + RoleBinding bound cluster-wide
Pod Security Admission
explanation: Because the task names a specific namespace and a namespaced resource (pods), a Role plus a RoleBinding in the frontend namespace is correct. A ClusterRoleBinding would grant access cluster-wide, and Pod Security Admission governs pod security context, not RBAC permissions.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — The foundation of RBAC

question: What happens when a subject has no RBAC binding that grants a requested action?
choices: The API server returns 403 Forbidden because RBAC is additive with no deny rules
A deny rule must explicitly block it
The action is allowed by default
The request is queued until a binding is created
explanation: Kubernetes RBAC is purely additive — there are no deny rules. With no matching binding, the default answer is 403 Forbidden (secure by default). It is never allow-by-default, and there is no queuing behavior.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — The foundation of RBAC

question: Which command verifies whether the service account 'kube-explorer' in the default namespace can delete pods?
choices: kubectl get clusterrolebinding kube-explorer
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:kube-explorer
kubectl describe sa kube-explorer
kubectl auth reconcile
explanation: kubectl auth can-i with the --as impersonation flag and the full service account principal (system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>) asks the API server (via a SubjectAccessReview) whether that action is permitted. Describing the SA or listing bindings shows configuration but doesn't evaluate the effective allow/deny decision.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Checking API access with can-i

question: You need to bind a reusable set of permissions defined cluster-wide, but limit them to a single namespace. What is the correct approach?
choices: Create a Role that copies the ClusterRole's rules
Bind the ClusterRole using a RoleBinding in that namespace
Use a ClusterRoleBinding and add a namespace field
Aggregate the ClusterRole into the admin role
explanation: Binding a ClusterRole with a RoleBinding scopes those permissions to just the namespace where the RoleBinding lives — the DRY hybrid pattern. A ClusterRoleBinding can't be namespace-scoped (the field is ignored), copying rules defeats reuse, and aggregation merges roles rather than scoping them.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Cluster-wide permissions

question: Which kubectl verbosity level best reveals the raw HTTP request, headers, bearer token, and response body for RBAC debugging?
explanation: -v=8 prints the curl-equivalent request including headers (the authorization bearer token) and a truncated response body — ideal for RBAC and auth debugging. (Use -v=9 for the full untruncated body.) -v=6 shows the URL and HTTP status code, while levels 2 and 4 are standard operational logs without the HTTP wire detail.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Accessing resources with kubectl -v

question: For a highly available control plane, why are odd numbers of etcd members (3, 5, 7) recommended?
choices: They reduce disk usage
Even numbers are not supported by Raft
They prevent split-brain and maximize fault tolerance because quorum needs a majority
They allow faster image pulls
explanation: etcd's Raft protocol requires a majority (quorum = N/2 + 1) to make decisions; odd numbers avoid split-brain and give the best fault tolerance per node. A 3-node cluster survives losing 1; a 2-node cluster is worse than 1 because losing either node loses quorum. The other options are unrelated to consensus.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Introduction to high availability

question: In a stacked-etcd HA topology, where does etcd run?
choices: On dedicated external hosts separate from the API servers
As a local static pod on each control plane node, managed by kubeadm
Inside the kube-proxy DaemonSet
As a Deployment in the kube-system namespace
explanation: In the stacked topology each control plane node runs its own etcd as a local static pod, and kubeadm manages etcd membership as nodes join — simpler and cheaper for medium clusters. External etcd runs on dedicated hosts. etcd is never part of kube-proxy, and the control plane components are static pods, not Deployments.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Introduction to high availability

question: Which set of credentials must accompany an 'etcdctl snapshot save' command?
choices: --cacert, --cert, and --key with the endpoint
--username and --password
An admin.conf kubeconfig
A bootstrap token
explanation: etcd requires full TLS authentication, so the snapshot command must pass --cacert (validates etcd's identity), --cert (proves your admin rights), and --key (authenticates the session), plus the endpoint (https://127.0.0.1:2379). etcdctl talks to etcd directly, not through kubeconfig, usernames, or bootstrap tokens.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Disaster recovery

question: When restoring an etcd snapshot, why must you restore to a NEW data directory rather than the live one?
choices: To save disk space
Because overwriting the active directory while etcd is running corrupts the transaction tables
The live directory is read-only
etcdctl cannot read the live directory
explanation: Restoring into the running database's active directory while the API server is still writing corrupts the transaction/page tables. The correct workflow restores to a new empty directory (e.g., /var/lib/etcd-restored), then repoints etcd.yaml's hostPath to it. Disk space and read-only attributes are not the reason.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Disaster recovery

question: What is the correct order for upgrading a kubeadm cluster?
choices: Worker nodes first, then the control plane
All nodes simultaneously
Control plane first, then worker nodes, one minor version at a time
Skip directly to the newest available version
explanation: You upgrade the control plane first (kubeadm upgrade plan/apply), then each worker (kubeadm upgrade node), advancing one minor version at a time and never skipping versions. Upgrading workers first or jumping multiple versions violates the version-skew policy and breaks the cluster.

question: Before upgrading the kubelet on a node during a cluster upgrade, which command should you run, and what does --ignore-daemonsets do?
choices: kubectl cordon; it deletes DaemonSet pods
kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets; it allows the drain to proceed because DaemonSet pods can't be evicted
kubectl delete node; it removes the node from etcd
kubectl taint node; it blocks all pods including system pods
explanation: You drain the node to safely evict workloads and cordon it; --ignore-daemonsets is required because DaemonSet-managed pods can't be evicted and would otherwise block the drain. cordon alone doesn't evict, deleting the node is destructive, and tainting isn't the upgrade procedure.

question: In Helm, what is the distinction between a chart and a release?
choices: A chart is the running instance; a release is the package
They are synonyms
A release is a repository of charts
A chart is the package (templates + values); a release is a specific running instance of that chart
explanation: A chart is the package — Chart.yaml metadata, templates, and values.yaml. A release is a specific deployed instance of that chart in a cluster; Helm tracks release history so you can 'helm rollback'. The terms are not interchangeable, and a release is not a repository.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Templating with Helm

question: How do you apply a Kustomize overlay directly with kubectl?
choices: kubectl apply -f overlays/dev
kubectl apply -k overlays/dev
helm install overlays/dev
kubectl kustomize apply overlays/dev
explanation: Kustomize is built into kubectl via the -k flag: 'kubectl apply -k overlays/dev' builds and applies in one step (use 'kubectl kustomize overlays/dev' to preview the rendered YAML). -f applies a single file without overlay processing, helm is a different tool, and 'kubectl kustomize apply' is not valid syntax.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — Layering with Kustomize

question: Running 'kubectl get certificates' returns an error that the resource type isn't found. After installing the cert-manager operator manifest, what changes?
choices: Nothing — certificates are a built-in resource
The operator registers CRDs so the API recognizes 'certificates', and a controller runs the reconciliation loop
kube-proxy starts managing certificates
The API server must be restarted manually to load the new type
explanation: Installing the operator manifest registers CustomResourceDefinitions (adding the 'certificates' type to the API) and deploys the controller that watches them and runs the control loop. 'certificates' is not built in, kube-proxy is unrelated, and the API server picks up new CRDs dynamically without a manual restart.
source: CKA Advanced Cluster Configuration — CRDs and the operator pattern

question: Which command quickly generates a syntactically correct deployment manifest without creating anything in the cluster?
choices: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl run web --image=nginx
kubectl edit deployment web
explanation: --dry-run=client -o yaml builds the manifest locally and prints valid YAML without contacting the API server, giving a correct starting template to redirect to a file and edit. 'apply' requires an existing file, 'run' creates a live bare pod, and 'edit' modifies an existing resource.
source: Working with Your Cluster — Working with Manifests and dry-run

question: Which control plane component watches for newly created pods with no assigned node and selects a node for them?
choices: kube-scheduler
kube-apiserver
kube-controller-manager
kubelet
explanation: The kube-scheduler is responsible for assigning nodes to newly created pods based on resource requirements and constraints. The kube-apiserver only accepts and serves requests, the controller-manager runs reconciliation loops, and the kubelet executes pods on the node.

question: A deployment's desired replica count is updated from 3 to 5. Which component detects this change and creates the new pods?
choices: kube-scheduler
kube-controller-manager
kubelet
kube-proxy
explanation: The kube-controller-manager runs the deployment and replica set controllers, which detect the state change and create the new pods to meet the desired state. The scheduler only places them, the kubelet runs them, and kube-proxy handles network routing.

question: What happens if the kubelet on a worker node is stopped or crashes?
choices: All pods on the node are immediately terminated
The API server assumes the kubelet's duties
The node continues running existing pods but cannot accept new ones, and eventually becomes NotReady
The container runtime shuts down automatically
explanation: The kubelet is the node agent that communicates with the control plane. If it stops, existing pods keep running via the container runtime, but the node cannot report its status. After the node-monitor-grace-period, the control plane marks it NotReady. It does not terminate pods immediately or affect the runtime.

question: How does a kubelet authenticate to the API server during node registration?
choices: Using a pre-shared static password configured in kubelet.conf
Using an anonymous SSH connection
Using the API server's cluster IP address
Using a TLS client certificate generated via the TLS bootstrapping process
explanation: The kubelet uses TLS client certificates to authenticate to the API server. During kubeadm join, TLS bootstrapping is used to securely generate and sign this certificate. Static passwords and anonymous connections are not used for node auth.

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes kube-proxy's role from the CNI's role?
choices: kube-proxy implements Kubernetes Services and load balancing; CNI assigns pod IPs and handles pod-to-pod routing
kube-proxy gives pods IP addresses; CNI implements Services
kube-proxy configures the DNS server; CNI routes external traffic
kube-proxy runs only on the control plane; CNI runs only on workers
explanation: kube-proxy maintains network rules on nodes to implement Kubernetes Services (ClusterIP, NodePort), allowing communication to backend Pods. The CNI plug-in is responsible for pod networking, including IP assignment and base pod-to-pod connectivity. Roles are not inverted, and both run on all nodes.

question: Why is etcd referred to as a consistent and highly-available key value store?
choices: It stores all application databases directly on the nodes
It uses the Raft consensus algorithm to maintain cluster state across multiple nodes securely
It automatically scales up nodes when CPU usage is high
It caches container images for faster startup
explanation: etcd uses the Raft protocol to ensure data consistency across multiple nodes, making it highly available for storing all Kubernetes cluster data and state. It is not an application database, an autoscaler, or an image cache.

question: If you directly modify a resource via etcdctl instead of using the API server, what is the consequence?
choices: The cluster state becomes instantly corrupted
The API server automatically syncs and validates the change post-modification
The change bypasses admission controllers, validation, and RBAC, risking cluster stability
It is the recommended way to resolve conflicting state
explanation: The API server enforces RBAC, validation, and admission control. Modifying etcd directly bypasses all safety checks, which can lead to invalid configurations and cluster instability. It is never recommended for normal operation.

question: You need to grant a user permission to view pods and services in the 'dev' namespace. Which RBAC resources are required?
choices: A ClusterRole and a ClusterRoleBinding
A RoleBinding in the 'default' namespace pointing to a ClusterRole
A PodSecurityPolicy and a Role
A Role in the 'dev' namespace and a RoleBinding in the 'dev' namespace
explanation: Permissions restricted to a specific namespace for namespaced resources (pods, services) require a Role and a RoleBinding in that specific namespace. ClusterRoles/Bindings apply globally, and PSPs are deprecated/removed security constraints.

question: A developer can create deployments in the 'test' namespace but gets a 403 Forbidden when trying to list nodes. Why?
choices: Nodes are cluster-scoped resources and their RoleBinding only grants permissions in the 'test' namespace
The developer's certificate has expired
The nodes are currently NotReady
Deployments are in a different API group than nodes
explanation: Nodes are cluster-scoped resources. A RoleBinding in a namespace cannot grant access to cluster-scoped resources; a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding are required. Certificate expiry causes 401 Unauthorized, and node readiness doesn't affect RBAC.

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Role from a ClusterRole?
choices: A Role defines deny rules; a ClusterRole defines allow rules
A Role grants permissions within a specific namespace; a ClusterRole grants cluster-wide permissions or access to cluster-scoped resources
A Role is used for service accounts; a ClusterRole is for users
A Role manages pods; a ClusterRole manages nodes
explanation: Roles are always confined to a specific namespace, whereas ClusterRoles apply cluster-wide and can grant access to cluster-scoped resources (like nodes) or non-resource endpoints. RBAC is additive (no deny rules), and both can be bound to users or service accounts.

question: When defining an RBAC rule for Deployments, which apiGroups value must be used?
choices: [''] (core group)
['extensions']
['apps']
['batch']
explanation: Deployments belong to the 'apps' API group. The core group ('') is for resources like Pods and Services. 'extensions' is deprecated for Deployments, and 'batch' is for Jobs/CronJobs.

question: If you want to grant read-only access to all core resources (Pods, Services, ConfigMaps), what should the verbs list contain?
choices: ['read', 'view']
['get', 'describe']
['get', 'list', 'watch']
explanation: In Kubernetes RBAC, read-only operations map to the verbs 'get', 'list', and 'watch'. 'read' and 'view' are not valid verbs, '*' grants full access, and 'describe' is a kubectl command that uses get/list under the hood, not an API verb.

question: By default, what happens when a pod is created without explicitly specifying a service account?
choices: It is assigned the 'default' service account in its namespace, and its token is automatically mounted
It runs anonymously without any API access
It is assigned the 'default' service account in its namespace, which has full admin privileges
The pod creation fails validation
explanation: Pods are automatically assigned the 'default' service account of their namespace, and the ServiceAccount admission controller automounts its token to /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount. The default SA has very limited permissions, not admin rights.
source: Kubernetes docs — Configure Service Accounts for Pods

question: A pod does not need to communicate with the API server. How can you improve security by preventing the service account token from being mounted?
choices: Delete the default service account
Set automountServiceAccountToken: false in the Pod or ServiceAccount spec
Use a NetworkPolicy to block API server egress
Set mountToken: disabled in the kubelet config
explanation: Setting automountServiceAccountToken: false prevents the kubelet from projecting the token into the pod's filesystem, reducing the attack surface. Deleting the default SA breaks pod creation, and NetworkPolicies are a broader networking tool, not the direct way to handle token mounts.
source: Kubernetes docs — Configure Service Accounts for Pods

question: Which command allows an administrator to test if the service account 'app-sa' can create deployments in the 'prod' namespace?
choices: kubectl get deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:app-sa
kubectl auth check create deployments --serviceaccount=app-sa
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n prod --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:app-sa
kubectl describe rolebinding app-sa
explanation: kubectl auth can-i evaluates authorization. By combining the action (create deployments), the namespace (-n prod), and the impersonation flag (--as=system:serviceaccount:prod:app-sa), it accurately queries the API server's SubjectAccessReview endpoint. The other commands are either invalid syntax or do not perform a definitive access check.

question: You are running 'kubeadm init' and want to ensure the control plane nodes use a specific network interface for cluster communication. Which flag is required?
choices: --control-plane-endpoint
--node-ip
--pod-network-cidr
--apiserver-advertise-address
explanation: --apiserver-advertise-address binds the API server to a specific IP address (and thus interface) for cluster communication. --control-plane-endpoint sets the shared endpoint for HA, --node-ip is a kubelet flag, and --pod-network-cidr defines the internal pod IP range.

question: After 'kubeadm init' completes successfully, what is the critical manual step required before you can use kubectl as a regular user?
choices: Copy /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf to ~/.kube/config and change its ownership
Install a CNI plugin
Reboot the control plane node
Run kubeadm join on the same node
explanation: To use kubectl, you must set up your kubeconfig by copying /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf to your home directory (~/.kube/config) and updating ownership. CNI installation is the next cluster setup step, but copying the config is required to even run the kubectl command.
source: Kubernetes docs — Creating a cluster with kubeadm

question: A worker node fails to join the cluster, and the logs show 'token expired'. What is the default lifespan of a kubeadm bootstrap token?
choices: 1 hour
24 hours
7 days
Never expires
explanation: By default, kubeadm bootstrap tokens expire after 24 hours for security reasons. You must generate a new one using 'kubeadm token create' if you need to add nodes after this period. They do not last indefinitely or for a single hour.

question: When upgrading a kubeadm cluster from v1.28.x to v1.29.y, which OS package must be upgraded first on the control plane node?
choices: kubelet
kubectl
kubeadm
containerd
explanation: kubeadm manages the upgrade process. Therefore, you must upgrade the kubeadm package first, then run 'kubeadm upgrade apply', and finally upgrade the kubelet and kubectl packages. Reversing this order breaks the upgrade workflow.

question: What is the maximum allowed version skew between the kube-apiserver and the kubelet?
choices: They must be exactly the same version
The kubelet can be newer than the apiserver
The kubelet can be up to one minor version older than the apiserver
The kubelet can be up to three minor versions older than the apiserver
explanation: As of recent releases, the kubelet can be up to three minor versions older than the kube-apiserver (e.g., apiserver 1.29, kubelet 1.26). It cannot be newer. Previously it was two versions, but it is explicitly supported to allow easier node upgrades.

question: A cluster administrator notices control plane certificates expire in 30 days. Which command safely renews all locally managed certificates?
choices: kubeadm certs renew all
kubectl certificate approve
kubeadm upgrade apply
systemctl restart kubelet
explanation: kubeadm provides the 'kubeadm certs renew all' command to manually renew control plane certificates (apiserver, etcd, etc.) for another year. 'kubectl certificate approve' is for CSRs, and while upgrades do renew certs, 'certs renew' is the direct operational command.
source: Kubernetes docs — Certificate Management with kubeadm

question: After running 'kubeadm certs renew all', the API server continues to present the old certificate. Why?
choices: The new certificates are pending approval in etcd
The static pods must be restarted so the components load the new files from disk
The kubelet needs to be upgraded
You must reboot the node
explanation: Renewing certificates updates the files on disk in /etc/kubernetes/pki. Control plane components like the API server load certs at startup; they must be restarted (e.g., by temporarily moving their manifests out of /etc/kubernetes/manifests and back) to pick up the new certificates. Node reboot is extreme and unnecessary.
source: Kubernetes docs — Certificate Management with kubeadm

question: You create a static pod by placing a manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests. How do you delete this pod?
choices: kubectl delete pod <name>
kubectl delete -f <manifest>
Remove the manifest file from the directory
systemctl stop kubelet
explanation: Static pods are managed directly by the kubelet, not the API server. Removing the manifest file from the watch directory instructs the kubelet to terminate the pod. 'kubectl delete' will only delete the mirror pod on the API server, which the kubelet will immediately recreate.

question: When taking an etcd snapshot, which flag specifies the location of the etcd server?
choices: --server
--cluster
--host
--endpoints
explanation: etcdctl requires the '--endpoints' flag (e.g., --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379) to know which etcd member to connect to. '--server' is used by kubectl, not etcdctl.

question: You execute 'etcdctl snapshot save snap.db'. How do you verify the snapshot is valid and not corrupted?
choices: etcdctl snapshot status snap.db
etcdctl snapshot verify snap.db
cat snap.db
kubectl get etcdsnapshot
explanation: The 'etcdctl snapshot status snap.db' command reads the snapshot file and outputs metadata (hash, revision, total keys), effectively verifying it is a valid, readable etcd snapshot. There is no 'verify' command, and catting binary data is useless.

question: During an etcd restore process on a kubeadm cluster, which file must be modified to point the etcd static pod to the new restored data directory?
choices: /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
/var/lib/etcd/config.yaml
/etc/etcd/etcd.conf
explanation: The kubeadm-managed etcd runs as a static pod. To use the newly restored data directory, you edit the hostPath volume in '/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml'. The kubelet detects the change and restarts the etcd pod automatically.

question: Why must you stop the API server before restoring an etcd snapshot?
choices: To prevent etcdctl from hanging
To clear the API server cache
To ensure no new state is written to etcd during the restore, preventing data corruption or inconsistency
Because the API server holds a lock on the snapshot file
explanation: If the API server is running, it may attempt to write new data while you are swapping out the backend store, leading to race conditions or split state. Stopping the API server ensures a clean cutover to the restored snapshot.

question: In a highly available control plane setup, what is the role of the external load balancer?
choices: To distribute external traffic to worker node NodePorts
To load balance etcd replication traffic
To provide ingress routing for HTTP applications
To route kubectl and worker node traffic evenly across multiple kube-apiserver instances
explanation: The control plane load balancer provides a single, stable IP/DNS endpoint (used in --control-plane-endpoint) for worker nodes and external clients to communicate with the multiple active kube-apiserver instances. It does not handle ingress or etcd replication.

question: Which kubeconfig field defines the active combination of cluster, user, and namespace?
choices: current-context
active-cluster
default-user
preferences
explanation: The 'current-context' field in a kubeconfig file points to the name of a context, which dictates which cluster to connect to, which user credentials to send, and which namespace to use by default.
source: Kubernetes docs — Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files

question: You have a kubeconfig file for a dev cluster and one for a prod cluster. How can you use them together without modifying the files?
choices: kubectl merge dev.conf prod.conf
Set KUBECONFIG=dev.conf:prod.conf
Run them in different namespaces
Set KUBE_CLUSTERS=dev,prod
explanation: By setting the KUBECONFIG environment variable to a colon-separated list of file paths (e.g., KUBECONFIG=dev.conf:prod.conf), kubectl merges them in memory at runtime. There is no 'kubectl merge' command.
source: Kubernetes docs — Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files

question: Which command generates the YAML for a NodePort service exposing a deployment named 'web' on port 80, without creating it?
choices: kubectl create service nodeport web --tcp=80:80
kubectl get service web -o yaml > new.yaml
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 --type=NodePort --dry-run=client -o yaml
kubectl run web --expose --port=80
explanation: The imperative 'kubectl expose' command combined with '--dry-run=client -o yaml' builds the Service manifest based on the deployment's selectors and outputs it as YAML without sending it to the API server. The other options either create live resources or are invalid syntax for this task.

question: You need to extract only the IP addresses of all pods. Which output format is most efficient?
choices: -o yaml
-o wide
-o json
-o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.podIP}'
explanation: JSONPath allows you to query and extract specific fields directly from the API response, avoiding heavy bash parsing. '-o wide' includes IPs but also much other text, while yaml/json dumps the entire objects.

question: Which kubectl flag allows you to define a tabular output with specific fields as columns?
choices: -o custom-columns
--sort-by
--show-labels
-o name
explanation: '-o custom-columns' lets you define column headers and map them to JSONPath expressions (e.g., -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,IP:.status.podIP) to create custom tables. '--sort-by' orders rows but doesn't define columns.

question: You want to update a Helm release named 'frontend' with a new values file. Which command is correct?
choices: helm apply frontend -f values.yaml
helm upgrade frontend myrepo/frontend -f values.yaml
helm install frontend --update
kubectl helm upgrade frontend
explanation: The 'helm upgrade' command is used to update an existing release to a new version of a chart or with new configuration values (passed via -f). 'helm apply' does not exist, and helm is a standalone binary, not a kubectl subcommand.

question: A Helm upgrade fails and causes application downtime. How do you quickly revert to the previous working state?
choices: helm uninstall <release-name> && helm install
kubectl undo deployment
helm rollback <release-name>
helm downgrade <release-name>
explanation: Helm tracks the history of releases. 'helm rollback <release-name>' seamlessly reverts the release to the previous revision. Uninstalling destroys resources (like PVCs), and 'helm downgrade' is not a valid command.

question: In a Kustomize directory structure, what is the purpose of the 'base' directory?
choices: It holds the final generated YAML output
It contains the environment-specific configurations like dev or prod
It stores the Helm chart templates
It contains the common, unmodified resource manifests shared across multiple environments
explanation: In Kustomize, the 'base' directory holds the core, unmodified YAML manifests. Overlays (like dev or prod) reference this base and apply environment-specific patches. It is unrelated to Helm.
source: Kubernetes docs — Declarative Management using Kustomize

question: To use Kustomize features natively within kubectl, which flag must you use?
choices: -k
-f
--kustomize
-R
explanation: The '-k' flag (or --kustomize) tells kubectl to process a directory containing a kustomization.yaml file. '-f' is for standard files/directories without kustomize processing.
source: Kubernetes docs — Declarative Management using Kustomize

question: What is the primary function of a CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) in Kubernetes?
choices: To replace standard resources like Deployments with faster versions
To extend the Kubernetes API with user-defined resource types
To define network routing rules for external traffic
To monitor cluster performance and generate alerts
explanation: A CRD allows users to extend the Kubernetes API by defining new, custom resource types (e.g., 'Certificates', 'Prometheuses') that can be managed via kubectl just like native resources. It does not replace core resources or handle networking directly.

question: Before shutting down a worker node for hardware maintenance, which command ensures no new pods are scheduled to it and gracefully evicts existing workloads?
choices: kubectl cordon <node>
kubectl taint node <node> maintenance=true:NoSchedule
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets
kubectl delete node <node>
explanation: 'kubectl drain' safely evicts pods, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets, and automatically cordons the node to prevent new pods. '--ignore-daemonsets' is required to bypass DaemonSets. Cordoning alone does not evict, and deleting the node causes abrupt termination.
source: Kubernetes docs — Safely Drain a Node

question: After hardware maintenance is complete, how do you allow the node to accept new pods again?
choices: systemctl restart kubelet
kubeadm join
kubectl undrain <node>
kubectl uncordon <node>
explanation: 'kubectl uncordon' removes the unschedulable taint/flag from the node, allowing the scheduler to place new pods on it. There is no 'undrain' command, and restarting the kubelet does not clear the unschedulable status in the API.
source: Kubernetes docs — Safely Drain a Node

question: Which CLI tool allows you to inspect running containers directly through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), bypassing the kubelet?
choices: crictl
docker
kubeadm
containerd
explanation: 'crictl' is the CLI tool for CRI-compatible container runtimes. It allows administrators to list and inspect pods, containers, and images directly for debugging. 'docker' is no longer the default runtime, and containerd is the runtime itself, not the standard generic CLI.

question: Why might you use 'crictl logs' instead of 'kubectl logs' during troubleshooting?
choices: Because crictl formats the logs in JSON
Because the API server or kubelet is down, preventing kubectl from fetching logs
Because crictl aggregates logs from all nodes
Because kubectl logs only works for control plane components
explanation: If the control plane, API server, or kubelet is broken, 'kubectl logs' will fail. 'crictl logs' talks directly to the local container runtime socket on the node, bypassing Kubernetes components, making it invaluable for debugging broken clusters.

question: What is a mandatory OS-level requirement for the kubelet to function correctly by default?
choices: SELinux must be in enforcing mode
A public IP address
Swap memory must be disabled
The firewalld service must be running
explanation: By default, the kubelet will fail to start if swap memory is enabled on the node. This ensures accurate memory accounting and QoS enforcement for containers. (While swap support is an alpha/beta feature in recent versions, disabling it remains the standard requirement.)

question: A cluster is deployed, but pods on different nodes cannot ping each other. The nodes are Ready. What component is missing or misconfigured?
choices: The kube-scheduler
CoreDNS
The ingress controller
The CNI plugin
explanation: The Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin handles cross-node pod-to-pod networking. Without a functional CNI, routing between nodes fails. CoreDNS relies on the network, and ingress handles external access, not internal pod routing.

question: Which command safely removes an etcd member from a running cluster before replacing the node?
choices: etcdctl member remove
kubectl delete pod etcd
kubeadm reset
systemctl stop etcd
explanation: To safely scale down or remove a node from an etcd cluster, you must use 'etcdctl member remove <id>'. Deleting the pod or stopping the service just marks the node as down, which degrades quorum. The member must be explicitly removed from the Raft consensus.

question: When defining an RBAC ClusterRole for reading namespaces, why is it unnecessary to specify a namespace in the binding?
choices: Namespaces are implicitly in the 'default' namespace
Namespaces are cluster-scoped resources, so they require a ClusterRoleBinding which does not take a namespace
The API server ignores namespaces for all read operations
Roles automatically fall back to cluster scope
explanation: Namespaces themselves are cluster-scoped resources (they don't belong to a namespace). Therefore, you must use a ClusterRole and a ClusterRoleBinding to grant access to them. ClusterRoleBindings apply globally and do not accept a namespace parameter.

question: How do you forcefully terminate a pod that is stuck in the 'Terminating' state due to a dead node?
choices: kubectl edit pod <name> and remove finalizers
kubectl drain the node
kubectl delete pod <name> --force
crictl rm <pod-id>
explanation: Using 'kubectl delete pod <name> --force' (which implies --grace-period=0) immediately removes the pod from the API server without waiting for confirmation from the kubelet. This is necessary when the underlying node is permanently unreachable.

question: A user executes 'kubectl get pods --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp'. In what order are the pods displayed?
choices: Newest pods first
Alphabetical by name
Random order
Oldest pods first
explanation: The --sort-by flag sorts results in ascending order based on the specified JSONPath field. For timestamps, ascending means oldest dates first.

question: You want to dry-run a kubectl command to ensure you have the correct RBAC permissions without actually making the change. Which flag should you use?
choices: --dry-run=server
--dry-run=client
--validate=false
--check-auth
explanation: '--dry-run=server' sends the request to the API server to run through authentication, authorization (RBAC), and validation admission controllers, but prevents the final persistence to etcd. '--dry-run=client' only processes locally and doesn't verify RBAC.

question: You need to run one log-collection pod on every node, and have it automatically appear on any node added to the cluster. Which controller should you use?
choices: Deployment
StatefulSet
DaemonSet
Job
explanation: A DaemonSet ensures one pod runs on every node and automatically schedules a pod onto newly added nodes — ideal for log collectors and monitoring agents. A Deployment/StatefulSet run a fixed replica count not tied to node count; a Job runs to completion and stops.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Choosing the Right Workload Controller

question: Which controller is best suited for a database that requires a stable identity and persistent storage per pod?
choices: StatefulSet
ReplicaSet
Deployment
DaemonSet
explanation: A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable, unique identity (e.g. db-0) plus persistent storage and ordered operations. Deployments and ReplicaSets treat pods as interchangeable; a DaemonSet pins one pod per node.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Choosing the Right Workload Controller

question: A Job is defined with completions: 6 and parallelism: 2. What happens?
choices: The Job runs pods until 6 complete successfully, at most 2 at a time
6 pods all run at once until 2 succeed
2 pods run, and the Job succeeds after either one completes
6 pods run forever, restarting on success
explanation: completions is the number of required successful runs (6) and parallelism caps concurrent pods (2), so it runs in batches of two until six succeed. Jobs stop once completions are met; they do not run forever.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Managing Batch Workloads

question: Which action will trigger a new rollout (new ReplicaSet) for a Deployment?
choices: Changing the replicas count from 3 to 5
Updating the container image in the pod template
Adding a label to the Deployment's metadata
Editing the Deployment's revisionHistoryLimit
explanation: Only changes to the pod template (such as the container image) create a new ReplicaSet and trigger a rollout. Changing replicas just scales; metadata labels and revisionHistoryLimit are deployment-spec fields that don't roll the pods.
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Updating a Deployment

question: In a RollingUpdate, what does maxSurge control?
choices: The maximum pods that can be unavailable during the update
The number of old ReplicaSets retained for rollback
The maximum extra pods allowed above the desired replica count during the update
How long Kubernetes waits before marking the rollout failed
explanation: maxSurge limits how many pods may run above the desired count while updating (default 25%). maxUnavailable limits pods offline; revisionHistoryLimit controls retained ReplicaSets; progressDeadlineSeconds governs failure timing.
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Controlling Updates with UpdateStrategy

question: A rollout to a bad image left the deployment broken. You need to return to the known-good revision 2. Which command does this?
choices: kubectl rollout status deployment app --revision=2
kubectl rollout history deployment app --revision=2
kubectl rollout undo deployment app --to-revision=2
kubectl scale deployment app --replicas=2
explanation: kubectl rollout undo --to-revision=2 scales down the current ReplicaSet and scales the revision-2 ReplicaSet back up. rollout history --revision=2 only inspects it; rollout status checks progress; scale changes replica count.
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Pausing and Rolling Back Deployments

question: Why should you define a readiness probe when using a RollingUpdate strategy?
choices: It speeds up the rollout by skipping unhealthy pods
It is required for Kubernetes to create a ReplicaSet
It lets the deployment stop the rollout if new pods aren't ready, protecting the running version
It encrypts the pod's configuration during the update
explanation: With a readiness probe, the deployment halts a rollout when too many new pods fail readiness (would breach maxUnavailable), keeping the previous version serving traffic. Without it, a pod is 'ready' at start and a broken rollout proceeds.
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Successfully Controlling Deployment Rollouts

question: You update a ConfigMap mounted as environment variables and want the running pods to use the new values. What must you do?
choices: Nothing — env vars hot reload automatically
Restart the pods, because env vars do not hot reload
Convert the ConfigMap to a Secret
Delete and recreate the ConfigMap with --reload
explanation: Environment variables do not hot reload; you must restart the pods (e.g. kubectl rollout restart) to pick up new values. Volume-mounted directories do support hot reloading, but env injection does not.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Decoupling Configuration

question: Which statement about Kubernetes Secrets is correct?
choices: Secret values are AES-encrypted in the manifest by default
Secret values are only Base64-encoded, which obscures but does not secure them
Secrets cannot be injected as environment variables
Anyone authorized to create a pod is automatically blocked from reading namespace Secrets
explanation: Secrets are Base64-encoded (easily decoded), not encrypted by default; enable etcd encryption at rest for real protection. They can be injected as env vars or volumes, and anyone who can create a pod in a namespace can read its Secrets.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Managing Secrets

question: Your HPA shows TARGETS as <unknown>/50% and is not scaling. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The deployment has too many replicas
maxReplicas is set too low
The HPA stabilization window is too short
The metrics server is unavailable or the pods lack resource requests
explanation: HPA needs the metrics server running and resource requests defined on the target pods to compute usage; <unknown> means metrics aren't available. Replica counts, maxReplicas, and the stabilization window don't cause <unknown> metrics.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Configuring HPA

question: A container repeatedly fails its livenessProbe. What does Kubernetes do?
choices: Restarts the container according to the pod's restart policy
Removes the pod's IP from the Service endpoints
Marks the node NotReady
Evicts every pod on the node
explanation: A failing livenessProbe causes the kubelet to restart the container per the restart policy. Removing the pod IP from Service endpoints is the readinessProbe behavior; liveness does not affect node status or evict other pods.
source: Managing the Kubernetes API Server and Pods — Defining Pod Health

question: A pod has requests and limits set so that CPU and memory requests exactly equal their limits. Which QoS class is assigned?
choices: BestEffort
Burstable
Guaranteed
Priority
explanation: Guaranteed QoS is assigned when requests equal limits for both CPU and memory — these pods are protected longest under resource pressure. Burstable is requests < limits; BestEffort is no requests/limits; Priority is not a QoS class.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Configuring Pod Admission

question: A container exceeds its configured memory limit. What happens?
choices: Its memory request is automatically increased
The pod is rescheduled to another node
The kernel terminates it and it shows OOMKilled
It is throttled and slowed down
explanation: Exceeding the memory limit causes the kernel to kill the process, giving an OOMKilled status. Throttling is what happens when a container exceeds its CPU limit, not its memory limit.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Defining Resource Limits

question: You add nodeSelector: disk=ssd to a pod, but no node has that label. What is the result?
choices: The pod schedules on a random node
The pod stays in Pending state
The scheduler creates the label automatically
The pod schedules on the control plane
explanation: nodeSelector is a hard requirement; with no matching node the pod remains Pending. Check kubectl get events / describe pod for a 'didn't match node selector' message. The scheduler never invents labels or ignores the selector.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Node Selection

question: You want three replicas of an app spread so no two run on the same node for high availability. Which mechanism achieves this?
choices: nodeSelector
A taint with NoExecute
A Pod Disruption Budget
Pod anti-affinity
explanation: Pod anti-affinity (with topologyKey kubernetes.io/hostname) tells the scheduler not to co-locate replicas with the same label on a node, spreading them for HA. nodeSelector pins to labels; taints repel pods; a PDB guards against voluntary disruptions, not placement.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Pod Anti-affinity

question: You create a static pod by placing a manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests. Which statement is true?
choices: You can delete it with kubectl delete pod
It is managed by the kubelet, and you remove it by deleting the manifest file
It is invisible from kubectl get pods
It is scheduled by the kube-scheduler like any other pod
explanation: Static pods are managed by the kubelet, not the API server; to remove one you delete its manifest from the staticPodPath. The kubelet creates a read-only mirror pod so it IS visible via kubectl, but kubectl delete won't remove it and the scheduler isn't involved.
source: Managing the Kubernetes API Server and Pods — Introducing and Working Static Pods

question: kubectl drain on a node fails with a message that eviction would violate a Pod Disruption Budget. What is a valid way to proceed?
choices: Delete the PDB's namespace
Scale the deployment up so the minAvailable floor is still met after eviction
Use kubectl cordon instead, which ignores PDBs
Set the pod's restartPolicy to Never
explanation: A PDB blocks evictions that would drop below its floor; scaling up the deployment so enough replicas remain lets the drain proceed. cordon only marks the node unschedulable (it doesn't evict or bypass PDBs), and restartPolicy is unrelated.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Protect Pods with PDBs

question: You need to generate a deployment manifest without sending it to the cluster. Which command should you use?
choices: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml
kubectl run deployment web --image=nginx --manifest-only
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 -o yaml
kubectl generate deployment web --image=nginx > deploy.yaml
explanation: Using --dry-run=client -o yaml generates the resource manifest locally without sending it to the API server. run is for pods (not deployments); expose creates a Service; generate is not a valid kubectl command.

question: A deployment has maxUnavailable: 1 and maxSurge: 1. With replicas: 3, what is the maximum number of pods running during an update?
explanation: maxSurge allows extra pods above the desired replicas count during a rollout. With replicas=3 and maxSurge=1, the maximum number of running pods at any time is 4. The other choices incorrectly assess the surge limit.

question: You execute `kubectl rollout undo deployment app`. What is the result if no revision is specified?
choices: The deployment scales to zero replicas.
The deployment is paused indefinitely.
The deployment rolls back to the previous revision.
An error is returned stating a revision is required.
explanation: If no --to-revision is specified, rollout undo defaults to rolling back to the immediate previous revision. It does not scale to zero, pause the deployment, or require the revision flag.

question: You need a pod to consume all key-value pairs from a ConfigMap as environment variables. Which field is appropriate?
choices: valueFrom
configMapKeyRef
volumeMounts
envFrom
explanation: envFrom pulls all data keys from a ConfigMap or Secret as environment variables. valueFrom targets a single key via configMapKeyRef, while volumeMounts treats them as files (not env vars).

question: A ConfigMap is created with immutable: true. What happens if a user tries to modify its data?
choices: The update fails and the API server rejects the change.
The data is updated, but running pods do not see the change.
The ConfigMap is recreated automatically.
The kubelet restarts all pods using the ConfigMap.
explanation: Setting a ConfigMap to immutable prevents any updates to its data, protecting it from accidental changes. The API server will reject the modification. It does not update silently or trigger restarts.

question: You need to pull a private image from a registry. Which type of Secret must you create?
choices: kubernetes.io/tls
kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson
Opaque
kubernetes.io/service-account-token
explanation: The dockerconfigjson (or dockercfg) type is used to store registry credentials for image pulls. Opaque is for generic data, tls is for certificates, and service-account-token is for API access.

question: How are Secret values stored in an Opaque secret manifest when created imperatively?
choices: Encrypted using AES-256
Hashed with SHA-256
Base64-encoded
Plain text
explanation: In Secret manifests, values are Base64-encoded, which is easily decoded. They are not encrypted or hashed in the manifest itself, though they can be encrypted at rest in etcd.

question: A Job repeatedly fails. Which field limits how many times the Job will try to create a replacement pod?
choices: restartPolicy
activeDeadlineSeconds
parallelism
backoffLimit
explanation: backoffLimit dictates the number of retries for a failed Job before it is marked as failed. activeDeadlineSeconds limits total execution time; restartPolicy applies at the container level; parallelism dictates concurrent pods.

question: A CronJob has concurrencyPolicy: Forbid. What happens if the previous run hasn't finished when it's time for the next run?
choices: The new run starts alongside the old one.
The new run replaces the old run immediately.
The old run is paused until the new run completes.
The new run is skipped.
explanation: With Forbid, the CronJob skips the new run if the previous one is still executing. Allow permits concurrent runs, and Replace cancels the currently running job to start the new one. Pausing is not a valid behavior.

question: Why might a DaemonSet fail to schedule a pod on a newly added control plane node?
choices: The pod template lacks the proper toleration for the control plane taint.
DaemonSets are hard-coded to ignore control plane nodes.
The control plane node does not have the kubelet installed.
The nodeSelector field defaults to worker nodes.
explanation: Control plane nodes typically have a NoSchedule taint. A DaemonSet must include a matching toleration to schedule pods there. DaemonSets do not ignore control planes natively, nor do they default to worker nodes.

question: A StatefulSet with 3 replicas scales up to 4. In what order is the new pod created and named?
choices: It is given a random hash like web-7fg2x.
It is named web-4 and created immediately.
It is named web-4 after web-3 is Running and Ready.
It is named web-3, and created only if all other pods are Ready.
explanation: StatefulSets index starting from 0, so replicas are web-0, web-1, web-2. Scaling to 4 adds web-3. The StatefulSet waits until prior pods are Ready before starting the next one. They do not use random hashes.

question: What is the purpose of volumeClaimTemplates in a StatefulSet?
choices: To dynamically provision unique PersistentVolumeClaims for each replica.
To share a single PersistentVolume across all replicas.
To mount an existing ConfigMap into every pod.
To define ephemeral storage for cache data.
explanation: volumeClaimTemplates automatically creates a unique PersistentVolumeClaim for each pod in the StatefulSet (e.g., data-web-0). It is not for sharing a single volume, ConfigMaps, or ephemeral storage.

question: A ReplicaSet is configured with a label selector app: web. What happens if you manually create a bare pod with the label app: web?
choices: The bare pod is immediately deleted by the admission controller.
The ReplicaSet adopts it and terminates an existing pod if replicas are exceeded.
The ReplicaSet ignores it because it was not created by the template.
The bare pod fails to schedule due to a port conflict.
explanation: ReplicaSets use label selectors to manage pods. If a pod matches the selector, the ReplicaSet adopts it. If this pushes the count over the desired replicas, one pod will be terminated to maintain the state.

question: A pod has two init containers, init-A and init-B. What is their execution order?
choices: They run concurrently alongside the main containers.
They run in random order before the main containers.
They run sequentially: init-A must complete successfully before init-B starts.
They run concurrently, and the main container starts when both finish.
explanation: Init containers run sequentially in the order they are defined in the pod manifest. Each must run to completion successfully before the next one starts, unlike main containers which start concurrently.

question: What happens if an init container repeatedly fails?
choices: The pod is marked as Running and the main containers start.
The pod is Evicted and moved to another node.
The failing init container is bypassed.
The kubelet restarts the pod until the init container succeeds (unless restartPolicy=Never).
explanation: If an init container fails, the kubelet repeatedly restarts the pod (if restartPolicy allows) until the init container succeeds. The main containers will not start, and it is not bypassed or immediately evicted.

question: Two containers in the same pod need to exchange data via files. Which approach should be used?
choices: Use an emptyDir volume mounted in both containers.
Map the host filesystem directly to both containers.
They share the root filesystem automatically.
Expose a ClusterIP service between them.
explanation: An emptyDir volume provides ephemeral storage shared by all containers in a pod, perfect for file-based communication. Containers do not share root filesystems automatically, and host filesystem maps or Services are not ideal for simple pod-local sharing.

question: Which probe is designed to protect slow-starting applications from being killed before they complete initialization?
choices: readinessProbe
startupProbe
livenessProbe
initialDelaySeconds
explanation: The startupProbe disables liveness and readiness checks until it succeeds, giving slow-starting apps time to boot without being prematurely killed. initialDelaySeconds is a parameter, not a probe itself.

question: You define a readinessProbe using a tcpSocket. How does the kubelet evaluate the probe's success?
choices: It expects an HTTP 200 OK response from the port.
It runs a shell command and checks for an exit code of 0.
It attempts to open a TCP connection to the specified port.
It measures the latency of the network connection.
explanation: A tcpSocket probe succeeds if it can establish a TCP connection to the specified port. HTTP 200 is for httpGet, exit code 0 is for exec probes, and latency is not evaluated.

question: A pod has a CPU limit of 500m but no request. How does the scheduler handle this?
choices: The pod is rejected by the admission controller.
The pod receives a request of 0, making it lowest priority.
The pod's CPU request defaults to 500m for scheduling purposes.
The pod is scheduled only on nodes with no CPU pressure.
explanation: If a limit is set but no request is specified, Kubernetes automatically sets the request to equal the limit (500m in this case). It does not default to 0 or get rejected.

question: Which configuration results in a BestEffort QoS class for a pod?
choices: Requests are defined, but limits are omitted.
Requests equal limits for all resources.
Only memory limits are defined.
Requests and limits are both omitted for all containers.
explanation: BestEffort is assigned when no resource requests or limits are set for any container in the pod. Burstable is assigned if requests < limits or only some are set; Guaranteed is when requests == limits everywhere.
source: Kubernetes docs — Pod Quality of Service

question: A pod requires GPU hardware, so you add nodeSelector: gpu=true. What is a limitation of this approach compared to Node Affinity?
choices: nodeSelector cannot express soft/preferred requirements.
nodeSelector requires a dedicated DaemonSet to enforce.
nodeSelector only works on control plane nodes.
nodeSelector ignores taints.
explanation: nodeSelector is a strict, simple matching mechanism and cannot express preferred rules (soft affinity) or complex expressions like In/NotIn. It does not require a DaemonSet and applies to any node.
source: Kubernetes docs — Assigning Pods to Nodes

question: A pod defines preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution for a node label. What happens if no node has this label?
choices: The pod stays in Pending state.
The pod schedules on the node with the most available resources.
The pod scheduler crashes.
The pod is rejected by the API server.
explanation: preferredDuringScheduling is a soft requirement. If no node matches the preference, the scheduler simply ignores the rule and schedules the pod on an available node based on standard scoring criteria. It does not stay Pending.
source: Kubernetes docs — Assigning Pods to Nodes

question: You apply a NoExecute taint to a node. What happens to running pods on that node that lack a toleration?
choices: They continue running but receive no new traffic.
They are immediately stopped without a grace period.
They are evicted from the node.
They are scaled down by their Deployment.
explanation: A NoExecute taint causes running pods without a matching toleration to be evicted from the node. NoSchedule only prevents new pods from scheduling. The eviction respects the termination grace period; they aren't scaled down.

question: Which toleration allows a pod to tolerate any taint with a specific key, regardless of its value or effect?
choices: operator: Equal with value: '*'
effect: NoSchedule with operator: In
operator: Wildcard
operator: Exists without specifying a value or effect
explanation: Using operator: Exists for a key without defining the value or effect will match all taints that have that key. Equal requires an exact match, and Wildcard is not a valid operator.

question: When defining pod affinity, what is the role of the topologyKey field?
choices: It specifies the node label key used to define the boundaries of a failure domain.
It defines the maximum distance between pods in milliseconds.
It restricts the pod to specific cloud provider regions.
It links the pod to a PersistentVolume topology.
explanation: topologyKey determines the domain (e.g., node, zone) for evaluating affinity. For example, topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname evaluates rules at the individual node level. It is not limited to cloud regions or PVs.
source: Kubernetes docs — Assigning Pods to Nodes

question: You run `kubectl scale statefulset db --replicas=5`. What is required for this to succeed?
choices: The cluster must have an active metrics-server.
Nothing; it manually updates the desired replica count in the StatefulSet spec.
The StatefulSet must have an active HPA.
All existing pods must be fully ready before the command is accepted.
explanation: kubectl scale is a manual imperative command that directly updates the replicas field in the resource's spec. It does not rely on metrics-server, HPA, or wait for existing pods before updating the spec.

question: If you modify a static pod's manifest file in the staticPodPath directory, what occurs?
choices: You must restart the kubelet manually to apply the changes.
The API server rejects the update.
The kubelet automatically detects the change and restarts the pod.
A new pod is created alongside the old one.
explanation: The kubelet periodically scans the staticPodPath directory. When a manifest is changed, the kubelet automatically detects it and restarts the static pod with the new configuration without requiring a kubelet restart.

question: A PodDisruptionBudget defines minAvailable: 2 for a deployment with 3 replicas. What happens during a node drain?
choices: All pods are evicted immediately.
The node drain is blocked completely until the PDB is deleted.
The drain forces the deployment to scale up to 4 replicas.
Evictions proceed as long as at least 2 replicas remain running and healthy.
explanation: A PDB protects against voluntary disruptions (like drains). With minAvailable: 2, the drain process will evict pods one at a time, pausing if the running replica count would drop below 2. It does not scale the deployment.

question: Which statement is a requirement of the Kubernetes networking model?
choices: Pods reach each other using NAT-translated addresses
All Pods can communicate with all other Pods on all nodes without NAT, using real Pod IPs
Only Pods on the same node can communicate directly
Pods must use the node's IP address to communicate
explanation: The model requires all Pods to reach all Pods on every node using their real IPs with no NAT. NAT is explicitly disallowed; cross-node communication is required; Pods use their own real IPs, not the node's.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Kubernetes Network Model

question: Two containers run in the same Pod. How do they communicate with each other?
choices: Over localhost on different ports
Via the Pod's ClusterIP service
Each container gets its own Pod IP and they route between them
Through the node's bridge interface using separate IPs
explanation: Containers in a Pod share one network namespace and one IP, so they reach each other over localhost on different ports. They do not have separate IPs and do not need a Service to talk to each other.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Pod Networking Internals

question: What is the purpose of the pause (infrastructure) container in a Pod?
choices: It runs the main application workload
It load balances traffic to the Pod
It enforces NetworkPolicy rules for the Pod
It sets up and holds the Pod's network namespace so app containers can restart without losing the network stack
explanation: The pause container starts first, creates the network namespace, and owns it for the Pod's lifecycle, so application containers can restart without re-IPing the Pod. It does not run the app, load balance, or enforce policy.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Pod Networking Internals

question: Which component is responsible for implementing the Kubernetes networking model (interfaces, IP addressing, bridges/tunnels)?
choices: kube-proxy
The CNI plugin
CoreDNS
The kubelet's cgroup driver
explanation: Kubernetes defines the model but abstracts implementation to the CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, etc.). kube-proxy implements Services, CoreDNS provides DNS, and the cgroup driver is unrelated to networking.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — CNI

question: Which component implements Services on each node and runs as a DaemonSet?
choices: kube-proxy
kubelet
CoreDNS
etcd
explanation: kube-proxy implements Services (default iptables mode) and runs as a Pod via a DaemonSet, one per node. CoreDNS is DNS, kubelet manages Pods, etcd is the datastore.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Service Networking Internals

question: In a Service spec, which field specifies the port the application listens on inside the container?
choices: port
targetPort
nodePort
clusterIP
explanation: targetPort is the container/app port. port is the Service's own listening port for clients, nodePort is the port exposed on each node, and clusterIP is the virtual IP.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Defining Deployments and Services

question: What is the default Service type if none is specified?
choices: NodePort
LoadBalancer
ClusterIP
ExternalName
explanation: ClusterIP is the default and is internal-only. The other types must be explicitly requested.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — ClusterIP Internals

question: What is the default port range for a NodePort service?
explanation: NodePort uses 30000–32767 by default. A port can be auto-assigned from this range or set statically within it.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — NodePort Internals

question: When you create a Service of type LoadBalancer, which other service resources are also created?
choices: Only a ClusterIP
Only a NodePort
A NodePort and a ClusterIP
An ExternalName and a ClusterIP
explanation: LoadBalancer builds on the lower types: it also gets a NodePort and a ClusterIP. The cloud LB sends traffic to the NodePort, which forwards to the ClusterIP, which reaches Pods.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — LoadBalancer Internals

question: A Service must reference a service running outside the cluster by DNS name without proxying traffic. Which type fits?
choices: Headless service
ExternalName
NodePort
LoadBalancer
explanation: ExternalName creates a CNAME to an external DNS name with no selector and no proxying. A headless service returns Pod IPs; NodePort/LoadBalancer expose in-cluster Pods.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Other Types of Services

question: How do you define a headless service, and what does DNS return for it?
choices: Set type: ExternalName; DNS returns a CNAME
Set type: NodePort; DNS returns the node IPs
Omit the selector; DNS returns the ClusterIP
Set clusterIP: None; DNS returns the matching Pod IPs
explanation: A headless service has clusterIP: None. With selectors, DNS returns all matching Pod IPs so the client chooses. This is common with StatefulSets and databases.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Other Types of Services

question: A ClusterIP Service shows zero endpoints. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The Service selector does not match any running, ready Pod's labels
The cluster has no LoadBalancer integration
CoreDNS is not running
The nodePort is outside 30000–32767
explanation: Endpoints are created from Pods whose labels match the Service selector. No matching/ready Pods means no endpoints. LoadBalancer integration, CoreDNS, and nodePort range are unrelated to empty ClusterIP endpoints.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Understanding Services

question: What is the fully qualified DNS name of a Service named web in namespace prod?
choices: web.prod.pod.cluster.local
prod.web.svc.cluster.local
web.prod.svc.cluster.local
web.svc.prod.cluster.local
explanation: The Service FQDN pattern is service.namespace.svc.cluster.local, so web.prod.svc.cluster.local. The 'pod' segment is used for Pod records; the segment order in the other options is wrong.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Cluster DNS Records

question: Where is CoreDNS configured in a default Kubernetes cluster?
choices: A ConfigMap named coredns in the kube-system namespace
A Secret named coredns in the default namespace
The /etc/kubernetes/coredns.conf file on each node
A CRD named CoreDNSConfig
explanation: CoreDNS reads a ConfigMap named coredns in kube-system, mounted as the Corefile at /etc/coredns. It is not a Secret, a node file, or a CRD.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Cluster DNS

question: What is the default dnsPolicy for a Pod, and what does setting dnsPolicy: None require?
choices: Default is None; None requires nothing extra
Default is ClusterFirst; None requires a dnsConfig block defining nameservers/searches
Default is Default; None disables DNS entirely
Default is ClusterFirstWithHostNet; None inherits the node's resolver
explanation: ClusterFirst is the default (cluster domain to cluster DNS, rest to node DNS). dnsPolicy: None ignores cluster DNS and requires a dnsConfig. The literal value 'Default' means inherit from the node and is not the actual default.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Custom Pod DNS Configuration

question: Why is DNS preferred over environment variables for service discovery?
choices: Env vars only work for LoadBalancer services
Env vars are injected only for Services that existed at Pod startup, so later Services require recreating the Pod; DNS updates dynamically
DNS is faster than env vars at the kernel level
Env vars cannot store IP addresses
explanation: Service env vars are a snapshot at Pod startup; a Service created afterward won't appear until the Pod is recreated. DNS resolves dynamically without restarting Pods. The other claims are false.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Service Discovery

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes an Ingress resource from an Ingress controller?
choices: The Ingress resource defines the rules; the Ingress controller is the reverse proxy that implements them and must be deployed separately
The Ingress resource routes traffic; the controller only stores rules
Both are deployed automatically with every cluster
The Ingress controller defines hosts/paths; the resource forwards packets
explanation: The Ingress resource holds the rules (hosts, paths, TLS); the controller is the actual reverse proxy that reads them and routes traffic, and it must be installed (clusters don't ship one). The other options invert or misstate these roles.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Ingress Architecture

question: An Ingress rule uses pathType: Exact with path /blue. Which request matches?
choices: /Blue
/blue/1
/blue
/blueprint
explanation: Exact requires an exact, case-sensitive match. Only /blue matches. /Blue differs by case, and /blue/1 and /blueprint are different paths (those would only match under Prefix for /blue).
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Path-Based Routing

question: Which is a valid reason to use Ingress instead of a Layer-4 LoadBalancer service?
choices: Ingress can load balance UDP traffic by IP and port
Ingress works at Layer 7, enabling host- and path-based routing while fronting many services on one IP
Ingress always provisions a dedicated public IP per service
Ingress cannot terminate TLS
explanation: Ingress is Layer 7 (HTTP), supporting name-based vhosts and path routing and exposing many services behind one IP. LoadBalancer services are Layer 4 (one service per IP/port). Ingress can terminate TLS, and it is used for HTTP, not arbitrary UDP.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Why Use Ingress Rather Than Load Balancers

question: In the Gateway API, which resource defines protocol-specific routing rules and attaches to a Gateway?
choices: GatewayClass
HTTPRoute
IngressClass
Service
explanation: HTTPRoute (and TCPRoute, GRPCRoute, etc.) defines routing rules and attaches to a Gateway via parentRefs. GatewayClass defines the controller-backed class, IngressClass belongs to the older Ingress API, and a Service is a backend target.
source: Configuring and Managing Kubernetes Networking, Services, and Ingress — Ingress Architecture (Kubernetes docs)

question: How does a NetworkPolicy behave once it selects a Pod for the Ingress direction?
choices: It allows all ingress traffic to that Pod
Ingress becomes default-deny for that Pod, and only explicitly allowed traffic is permitted
It blocks all egress as well, automatically
It has no effect unless every namespace has a policy
explanation: Selecting a Pod for a direction flips that direction to default-deny; only traffic matched by the policy's rules is allowed. It does not affect egress unless Egress is in policyTypes, and policies are additive across namespaces.
